common_name: Quedlinburger Niederliegende Lemon Balm (Procumbent High-Oil Lemon Balm)

planting.note: Direct sow shallowly after the last frost once soil has warmed, or start indoors 6-8 weeks earlier for a head start; this German heirloom strain from Quedlinburg germinates like ordinary lemon balm but establishes with a distinctive ground-hugging first-year habit.

directions: This traditional German seed strain, named for the town of Quedlinburg near the Harz mountains, grows low and procumbent along the ground in its first year before shifting to a more upright habit in its second season, making it useful as a dense, aromatic groundcover as it matures. It carries a notably higher citronellal and essential-oil content than common lemon balm, giving a sharper lemon punch in teas and dried-herb blends, and it has proven more winter-hardy in trials than standard seed-grown lemon balm. Grow it exactly as you would ordinary lemon balm, in moist, well-drained soil with some afternoon shade in hot climates, and shear plants back after their pale yellowish-white flowers fade to renew fragrant foliage and curb self-seeding. Divide congested clumps every few years once the plant settles into its upright second-year form.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring (or fall in mild climates) in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this Cretan-origin selection is propagated vegetatively since seed does not reliably reproduce its distinct lime scent and softly pubescent foliage.

directions: Lime Balm traces to a wild population from Crete, sometimes classified as Melissa officinalis subsp. altissima, and is distinguished from ordinary lemon balm by its softly hairy, lime-green foliage that smells and tastes distinctly of lime rather than lemon, along with larger, showier light-lavender flower spikes that draw in bees. Site it in full sun to part shade in average, well-drained soil, giving it a little afternoon shade in hot-summer regions to keep the leaves from scorching. Harvest young leaves fresh for a citrusy herbal tea or infused syrup, and shear the plant back hard after flowering to encourage a flush of tender new growth and to prevent it from becoming leggy. Divide clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor, since named selections like this one are best kept true by division rather than seed.

common_name: Pikanta Summer Savory (Spicy Bush Summer Savory)

planting.note: Direct sow shallowly once soil has warmed after the last frost; this Central European seed strain is grown exactly like common summer savory but forms a denser, more compact bush.

directions: Pikanta is a Central European seed strain of summer savory selected for a dense, upright, bushy habit and a notably more intense, spicier flavor than common garden-strain summer savory, packing more peppery punch per leaf into bean, lentil, and meat dishes. Direct sow into lean, well-drained soil in full sun once the soil has warmed, thinning seedlings so the compact plants have room to branch fully. Its small oval leaves release a strong spicy aroma when brushed or crushed, and the plant's tidy dense form suits containers and small raised beds as well as open garden rows. Harvest whole stems for drying right as the small white-to-lilac flowers begin to open, when the essential-oil concentration and flavor intensity peak.
